title: Valid Word Abbreviation
statement:
Return `true` if the string `abbr` is an abbreviation of the string `word`, and `false` otherwise.

An abbreviation of `word` is made by choosing any number of non-empty substrings of `word` that neither overlap nor touch one another, and writing each chosen substring's length, in decimal and without leading zeros, in its place. Choosing nothing is allowed (then the abbreviation is `word` itself), and so is choosing the whole word.

Because chosen substrings never touch, every maximal run of digits in `abbr` is a single length. A run that begins with `0` (including a lone `0`) is therefore never part of a valid abbreviation.
constraints: word consists of only lowercase English letters
abbr consists of lowercase English letters and digits
Every number in abbr fits in a 32-bit signed integer
notes:
## Intuition

An abbreviation is a recipe for walking through `word`: a letter says "the next character must be this", and a number says "skip this many characters". So walk both strings at once with two pointers moving in the same direction: `i` in `word` and `j` in `abbr`. The answer is `true` exactly when the recipe uses up both strings at the same moment. (A slower check expands every number into that many wildcard characters and compares the result with `word` position by position.)

## Approach

1. Start with `i = 0` in `word` and `j = 0` in `abbr`.
2. While both pointers are inside their strings, look at `abbr[j]`.
3. If it is a digit: a leading `0` is never allowed, so return `false`. Otherwise read the whole run of digits into `skip` and advance `i` by `skip`.
4. If it is a letter, it must equal `word[i]`; if not, return `false`. Then advance both pointers.
5. After the loop, return `true` only if `i` is exactly `word.length` and `j` is exactly `abbr.length`.

## Example 1, step by step

`word = "internationalization"` (20 letters), `abbr = "i12iz4n"`. `i` matches `i` (`i = 1`, `j = 1`). The run `12` gives `skip = 12`, so `i = 13`, `j = 3`. `word[13]` is `i` and `word[14]` is `z`, both matching (`i = 15`, `j = 5`). The run `4` moves `i` to `19`, and `word[19]` is `n`, matching the final letter. Both pointers end at their lengths (20 and 7), so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(|word| + |abbr|): every step advances at least one pointer.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Reject a run that starts with `0` before parsing it; `"a01"` must not be read as a skip of 1.
- Read the whole run of digits (`12`, not `1` then `2`); after a number the next character of `abbr` is always a letter.
- A skip can jump past the end of `word`; the final check `i === word.length` catches it. In Java or C, `i + skip` can overflow `int` when `skip` is near `2^31 - 1`; use a `long` or compare `skip` with the letters left first.
- Both strings must be fully used: `("hi", "hi1")` and `("ab", "a1b")` are `false`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `i` | position in `word` of the next character to match |
| `j` | position in `abbr` of the next token to read |
| `skip` | the number written in the current run of digits |

narration.2: i is the next character of word that still has to be accounted for.
narration.3: j is the next character of abbr to read.
narration.4: Walk both strings together while neither is used up.
narration.5: A digit starts a length that skips characters of word.
narration.6: A length never starts with 0, so a leading zero makes abbr invalid.
narration.9: skip will hold the number written in this run of digits.
narration.10: Keep reading while the run of digits continues.
narration.11: Append this digit to the number.
narration.14: Jump over the skip characters of word that the number stands for.
narration.16: A letter in abbr must equal the current letter of word.
narration.17: A mismatched letter means abbr does not describe word.
narration.19: The letter matched: move on in word...
